cards.front: In AWS Organizations, what is the difference between the management account and a member account?
cards.back: The **management account** created the organization: it creates or invites accounts, attaches policies and pays the whole bill. **Member accounts** are all the others; each can belong to only **one** organization at a time.

cards.front: Name three billing benefits of consolidated billing in AWS Organizations.
cards.back: One bill for all accounts, **volume pricing** based on combined usage, and **Reserved Instance / Savings Plans discounts shared** across accounts. It costs nothing extra.

cards.front: How deep can organizational units be nested, and how many accounts does an organization allow by default?
cards.back: OUs can go **five levels** below the root. The default account quota is **10**, adjustable through Service Quotas.

cards.front: Does a service control policy grant permissions?
cards.back: No. An SCP only sets the **maximum** permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts. Someone still needs an IAM (or resource-based) policy that allows the action.

cards.front: Which principals are NOT restricted by SCPs?
cards.back: Users and roles in the **management account**, and **service-linked roles**. (The root user of a member account IS restricted.)

cards.front: What two rules decide whether an SCP hierarchy allows an action for an account?
cards.back: An **Allow** must exist at **every level** from the root through each OU to the account, and **no level** may have an explicit **Deny** for it.

cards.front: What is FullAWSAccess?
cards.back: The AWS managed SCP that allows all actions. It is attached to the root, every OU and every account when SCPs are enabled. Removing it without a replacement blocks everything below that level.

cards.front: Deny-list versus allow-list SCP strategy: which one blocks brand-new AWS services automatically?
cards.back: The **allow list** (detach FullAWSAccess, allow only approved services). The deny list keeps FullAWSAccess and blocks only what you name, so new services work by default.

cards.front: What are the current SCP size and attachment limits?
cards.back: Up to **10 SCPs** attached directly to a root, OU or account, and **10,240 characters** per SCP (raised in May 2026 from 5 and 5,120).

cards.front: How does a resource control policy (RCP) differ from an SCP?
cards.back: An SCP caps what **principals in your member accounts** can do. An RCP caps what can be done **to resources in your member accounts**, by any caller, including outsiders. Used for data perimeters.
cards.updated: RCPs were introduced in late 2024, after the course slides

cards.front: What do tag policies do, and what do they ignore?
cards.back: They standardize tag keys, capitalization and allowed values, can **block noncompliant tagging** on chosen resource types and produce compliance reports. **Untagged resources** and undefined keys are not evaluated.

cards.front: aws:SourceIp versus aws:RequestedRegion: what does each compare?
cards.back: `aws:SourceIp` = the public IP the call comes **from**. `aws:RequestedRegion` = the Region the call goes **to**.

cards.front: Why use BoolIfExists with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent in a Deny statement?
cards.back: Requests signed with long-term access keys carry no `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` key at all. `BoolIfExists` treats a missing key as a match, so those requests are denied too.

cards.front: Which resource ARN do s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject each need?
cards.back: `s3:ListBucket` → bucket ARN `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket` (bucket level). `s3:GetObject` → `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*` (object level).

cards.front: How do you let every account in your organization (including future ones) use an S3 bucket without listing account IDs?
cards.back: Bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` and a condition `aws:PrincipalOrgID` equal to your organization ID (o-xxxxxxxxxx).

cards.front: What happens to your own permissions when you assume an IAM role?
cards.back: You set them aside: the session has **only the role's permissions** until you switch back. With a resource-based policy, you keep your own permissions.

cards.front: For a cross-account request using a resource-based policy, which policies must allow it?
cards.back: **Both**: the resource-based policy in the owning account and an identity-based policy in the caller's account. (Within one account, either one is usually enough.)

cards.front: Which EventBridge targets classically use a resource-based policy, and which need an IAM execution role?
cards.back: Resource policy: **Lambda, SNS, SQS, CloudWatch Logs, API Gateway**. Execution role: e.g. **Kinesis Data Streams, ECS tasks, Step Functions, SSM Run Command**. Since 2025, Lambda/SNS/SQS can also use a role.
cards.updated: Execution roles supported for all targets since March 2025

cards.front: Which IAM entities can have a permissions boundary?
cards.back: **Users and roles** only, not groups. The boundary is an AWS managed or customer managed policy.

cards.front: Boundary allows s3:*, cloudwatch:*, ec2:*. Identity policy allows only iam:CreateUser. What can the user do?
cards.back: **Nothing.** Effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity policies, and they share no actions.

cards.front: A policy denies sqs:* and allows sqs:DeleteQueue. Can the user delete a queue?
cards.back: No. An **explicit deny always wins** over any allow.

cards.front: What is an IAM Identity Center permission set?
cards.back: A reusable template of IAM policies (managed, inline, optional boundary) plus a session duration. Assigning it to a user or group for an account makes Identity Center create a matching IAM role there.

cards.front: What can a user reach with one IAM Identity Center login?
cards.back: AWS accounts in the organization, pre-integrated and custom **SAML 2.0** business apps (Salesforce, Microsoft 365...), AWS managed apps, and EC2 Windows instances via Fleet Manager Remote Desktop.

cards.front: How does ABAC work in IAM Identity Center?
cards.back: User attributes (team, cost center, title) from the identity source are passed into the session as tags; policies compare `aws:PrincipalTag` with resource tags. Change the attribute, and access follows without editing policies.

cards.front: AWS Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD in one line each?
cards.back: **Managed Microsoft AD**: real AD in AWS, trusts, MFA. **AD Connector**: proxy to on-premises AD, stores nothing. **Simple AD**: basic Samba-based standalone directory, no trusts, no MFA (closed to new customers from 30 July 2026).
cards.updated: Simple AD no longer open to new customers from 30 July 2026

cards.front: Two ways to use a self-managed on-premises AD as the IAM Identity Center identity source?
cards.back: Create **AWS Managed Microsoft AD** with a **two-way trust** to the on-premises domain, or create an **AD Connector** that proxies to it.

cards.front: In AWS Control Tower, how are preventive, detective and proactive controls implemented?
cards.back: Preventive → **SCPs** (and RCPs). Detective → **AWS Config rules**. Proactive → **CloudFormation hooks** that check resources before provisioning.
cards.updated: Guardrails renamed controls; proactive type added

cards.front: What does AWS Control Tower set up for you?
cards.back: A governed **landing zone** on AWS Organizations (e.g. log archive and audit accounts), **Account Factory** for vending new accounts, **controls**, and a compliance **dashboard**, plus IAM Identity Center for sign-in by default (you can opt out).

cards.front: When AWS Organizations creates a new member account, how do administrators in the management account get into it?
cards.back: Organizations adds an IAM role, by default named **OrganizationAccountAccessRole**, with full admin rights and a trust policy naming the management account. Admins there assume (switch to) it. The role is still limited by the SCPs on that account.

cards.front: Which tool tells you whether a request would be allowed, without making the call, and what does it not evaluate?
cards.back: The **IAM policy simulator** (now in the IAM console). It evaluates identity policies, a permissions boundary, SCPs and a supplied resource policy, with condition values you set. It does **not** evaluate RCPs.
cards.updated: The simulator moved into the IAM console; the standalone policysim site is no longer maintained
